The shop is closer to reception, while toilets and baby-changing facilities are reached from the corridor between the two. You've settled on a topic for your psychology experiment, so talk me through it in your own words. We want to test whether background music affects how well students concentrate while reading. We considered studying sleep and attention, but collecting reliable sleep data seemed too ambitious for this assignment. Sensible. What first led you to the music question? Was it a paper from your reading list? We found a useful paper afterwards, but it wasn't where the idea came from. Megan and I both revised with music on, and we kept disagreeing about our own habit. She thinks songs help her focus. I usually end up listening to the words instead of studying. We wanted to investigate that disagreement properly. You gave us advice on narrowing the topic once we mentioned it, but the original suggestion was ours. Good distinction. A question that grows from observation can work well if the method is rigorous. What exactly will change between the groups? I'm asking for your independent variable. The reading period will be 12 minutes in every condition as well. We don't want task length to vary. Excellent. And your dependent measure? Saying concentration is too broad unless you define how you want to read. Immediately after reading, everyone will complete the same short comprehension test. Today's lecture introduces the science of sleep, a behavior so familiar that it is easy to underestimate its complexity. We spend roughly a third of our lives asleep. Scientists agree that sleep supports several biological processes, although no single explanation accounts for every feature of it. Rather than treating sleep as a period when the brain simply switches off, researchers now describe it as an active sequence of changing states. We will begin with the systems that regulate when we sleep. Two broad forces interact. One is sleep pressure, which generally increases the longer a person remains awake and declines during sleep. The other is timing information from an internal clock. This interaction explains why someone can feel extremely tired late at night, yet become temporarily more alert after sunrise. The brain normally increases production of a hormone called melatonin. Rising levels help us feel drowsy and signal that the biological night has begun. Melatonin does not act like a powerful sleeping drug, and taking more of it cannot compensate for every cause of poor sleep. Its central role is as a timing signal, coordinating the body's preparation for rest. That signal operates within a roughly 24-hour pattern known as the circadian rhythm. The central clock is located in a small region of the brain, but clocks in other tissues respond to its timing. Left entirely without external cues, the daily cycle may drift slightly. Exposure to daylight, especially in the morning, resets it each day and keeps it aligned with the local day-night schedule. Mealtimes and activity provide secondary cues, but light is the strongest one for most people. Artificial light can alter this process. Bright screens late in the evening may delay the normal rise in sleepiness, particularly if they are held close to the eyes. The effect varies among individuals and depends on brightness, duration and timing. This is why advice to reduce evening screen use is about preparing the clock for sleep, rather than claiming that any brief glance at a phone will cause a disorder. Once asleep, we move through a repeating pattern of stages. For a simple overview, these are often grouped into two main types, REM sleep and deep sleep. REM stands for rapid eye movement. Brain activity in this stage can resemble waking activity. Vivid dreaming is common and most large muscles are temporarily less active. Deep sleep belongs to non-REM sleep and is marked by especially slow, synchronized brain waves. A night's sleep contains several cycles and their composition changes towards morning. The stages contribute differently to restoration. Deep sleep is strongly associated with physical recovery. During it, the body repairs tissue, rebuilds muscle and releases growth hormone. Athletes therefore pay attention to sleep as part of training, but the same processes matter after ordinary daily activity. Deep sleep tends to be more abundant in the first portion of the night, which is one reason a severely shortened night cannot be fully repaired by simply lying in later once. REM sleep is particularly important for the brain. Evidence links it to emotional processing and to consolidating memory. The process through which newly learned material becomes more stable. Other sleep stages contribute to learning too, so it would be misleading to assign all memory work to REM alone. Still, experiments in which researchers interrupt selected stages show that the architecture of sleep matters, not just the total number of hours spent in bed. We can see this in students. Reading notes until very late may create extra study time, but reduced sleep can impair attention during the next day's test and make new learning less efficient. A regular pattern of study followed by adequate sleep generally supports recall better than an all night session, even though the student who stayed awake spent more hours looking at the material. Now consider the effects of insufficient sleep on health. Even several nights of restricted sleep can alter the activity of immune cells and weaken the immune system. That does not mean one late night guarantees an infection. It means that repeated shortage reduces one part of the body's defense and is associated with greater vulnerability over time. There are immediate psychological effects as well. Sleep loss has a strong influence on mood. Tired people often report greater irritability and anxiety, and they may react more strongly to minor difficulties. Attention and decision making can also suffer. These changes matter in workplaces involving driving, machinery or medical judgment, where a brief lapse can have serious consequences. Sleep needs vary with age and from person to person. Teenagers generally need more sleep than adults, partly because adolescence is a period of rapid growth. Their internal timing also tends to shift later, so many find it difficult to fall asleep early, even when school requires an early start. This biological tendency can conflict with social schedules. It should not automatically be interpreted as laziness. Adults sometimes assume that older people need almost no sleep. In fact, sleep may become lighter and more fragmented with age, but restorative sleep remains important. Daytime naps can be useful in some circumstances, although long or late naps may make it harder for a person with nighttime difficulties to settle at bedtime. Persistent difficulty sleeping deserves separate attention. Sleep disorder is insomnia, defined by repeated trouble falling asleep, staying asleep or obtaining restorative sleep, despite having an adequate opportunity to rest. It differs from choosing to stay awake for work or entertainment. Other disorders include breathing interruptions and abnormal movements, so treatment should depend on the cause rather than on one general remedy. For healthy sleep, consistency is often more useful than a dramatic weekend correction. Experts recommend keeping a regular bedtime and waking time, making the room dark and reasonably cool, and allowing a quiet transition from work to rest. Regular daytime activity can help, whereas vigorous exercise immediately before bed affects people differently. Diet and stimulants also matter. In particular, experts advise avoiding caffeine in the evening. It blocks signals associated with sleep pressure and can remain active in the body for many hours. Coffee is the obvious source, but tea, energy drinks, chocolate and some medicines may contain it too. Alcohol may initially make a person feel sleepy, yet it can disrupt the later structure of the night. The practical message is that good sleep depends on timing, environment and behaviour, as well as duration. In our next lecture, we will compare human sleep with the very different patterns found across the animal kingdom.

Bright screens late in the evening may delay the normal rise in sleepiness,
particularly if they are held close to the eyes.
The effect varies among individuals and depends on brightness, duration and timing.
This is why advice to reduce evening screen use is about preparing the clock for sleep,
rather than claiming that any brief glance at a phone will cause a disorder.
Once asleep, we move through a repeating pattern of stages.
For a simple overview, these are often grouped into two main types, REM sleep and deep sleep.
REM stands for rapid eye movement.
Brain activity in this stage can resemble waking activity.
Vivid dreaming is common and most large muscles are temporarily less active.
Deep sleep belongs to non-REM sleep and is marked by especially slow, synchronized brain waves.
A night's sleep contains several cycles and their composition changes towards morning.
The stages contribute differently to restoration.
Deep sleep is strongly associated with physical recovery.
During it, the body repairs tissue, rebuilds muscle and releases growth hormone.
Athletes therefore pay attention to sleep as part of training,
but the same processes matter after ordinary daily activity.
Deep sleep tends to be more abundant in the first portion of the night,
which is one reason a severely shortened night cannot be fully repaired by simply lying in later once.
REM sleep is particularly important for the brain.
Evidence links it to emotional processing and to consolidating memory.
The process through which newly learned material becomes more stable.
Other sleep stages contribute to learning too, so it would be misleading to assign all memory work to REM alone.
Still, experiments in which researchers interrupt selected stages show that the architecture of sleep matters,
not just the total number of hours spent in bed.
We can see this in students.
Reading notes until very late may create extra study time,
but reduced sleep can impair attention during the next day's test and make new learning less efficient.
A regular pattern of study followed by adequate sleep generally supports recall better than an all night session,
even though the student who stayed awake spent more hours looking at the material.
Now consider the effects of insufficient sleep on health.
Even several nights of restricted sleep can alter the activity of immune cells and weaken the immune system.
That does not mean one late night guarantees an infection.
It means that repeated shortage reduces one part of the body's defense and is associated with greater vulnerability over time.
There are immediate psychological effects as well.
Sleep loss has a strong influence on mood.
Tired people often report greater irritability and anxiety, and they may react more strongly to minor difficulties.
Attention and decision making can also suffer.
These changes matter in workplaces involving driving, machinery or medical judgment, where a brief lapse can have serious consequences.
Sleep needs vary with age and from person to person.
Teenagers generally need more sleep than adults, partly because adolescence is a period of rapid growth.
Their internal timing also tends to shift later, so many find it difficult to fall asleep early, even when school requires an early start.
This biological tendency can conflict with social schedules.
It should not automatically be interpreted as laziness.
Adults sometimes assume that older people need almost no sleep.
In fact, sleep may become lighter and more fragmented with age, but restorative sleep remains important.
Daytime naps can be useful in some circumstances, although long or late naps may make it harder for a person with nighttime difficulties to settle at bedtime.
Persistent difficulty sleeping deserves separate attention.
Sleep disorder is insomnia, defined by repeated trouble falling asleep, staying asleep or obtaining restorative sleep, despite having an adequate opportunity to rest.
It differs from choosing to stay awake for work or entertainment.
Other disorders include breathing interruptions and abnormal movements, so treatment should depend on the cause rather than on one general remedy.
For healthy sleep, consistency is often more useful than a dramatic weekend correction.
Experts recommend keeping a regular bedtime and waking time, making the room dark and reasonably cool, and allowing a quiet transition from work to rest.
Regular daytime activity can help, whereas vigorous exercise immediately before bed affects people differently.
Diet and stimulants also matter.
In particular, experts advise avoiding caffeine in the evening.
It blocks signals associated with sleep pressure and can remain active in the body for many hours.
Coffee is the obvious source, but tea, energy drinks, chocolate and some medicines may contain it too.
Alcohol may initially make a person feel sleepy, yet it can disrupt the later structure of the night.
The practical message is that good sleep depends on timing, environment and behaviour, as well as duration.
